stages.title: RESPONSIBLE GOVERNMENT: THE CONSTITUTIONAL MAP

groups.heading: UNION ARCHITECTURE
items: Articles 74-75: PM-led Council and collective responsibility.
Article 77: conduct of Union business.
Article 78: PM-President information duties.

groups.heading: STATE PARALLELS
items: Articles 163-164: CM-led Council and Assembly responsibility.
Articles 166-167: State business and information duties.
The architecture is parallel with bounded contextual differences.

groups.heading: SYSTEM LOGIC
items: Election creates the House.
House majority supports the ministry.
Continuing confidence sustains authority.

stages.answer_line: “Cabinet government” may name the constitutional form, while “cabinet dominance” or “prime-ministerial government” are later analytical claims about the internal distribution of power.

stages.title: NOMINAL HEAD, REAL EXECUTIVE AND BINDING ADVICE

groups.heading: FORMAL AND REAL POWER
items: The President is constitutional head.
The PM and Council form the real political executive.
Policy authority carries Lok Sabha responsibility.

groups.heading: ADVICE RULE
items: Article 74 advice normally binds.
The President may once require reconsideration.
Reconsidered advice binds.

groups.heading: BOUNDARIES
items: Article 74(2) protects inquiry into advice.
Underlying legality may still be reviewed.
Hung-House appointment and dissolution use convention and floor testing.

stages.answer_line: Courts may review the action on constitutional grounds while Article 74(2) protects the advice itself from inquiry.

stages.title: CLASSIC FEATURES AND COLLECTIVE RESPONSIBILITY

groups.heading: SYSTEM FEATURES
items: Dual executive and majority or coalition rule.
Executive drawn from legislature.
PM leadership and possible lower-House dissolution.

groups.heading: COLLECTIVE RULE
items: Cabinet decisions bind all ministers publicly.
A dissenting minister must accept or resign.
Loss of Lok Sabha confidence affects the entire ministry.

groups.heading: INDIVIDUAL RULE / LIMIT
items: A minister may leave for misconduct or failure.
Individual departure need not topple government.
Fusion does not erase courts, bicameralism or elections.

stages.answer_line: The President is normally a nominal executive, but bounded discretion and information rights prevent the office from becoming constitutionally irrelevant.

stages.title: CONFIDENCE, DISSOLUTION AND CARETAKER CONVENTIONS

groups.heading: GOVERNMENT FORMS
items: Majority ministry.
Coalition ministry.
Minority ministry with outside support.

groups.heading: CONFIDENCE TEST
items: No-confidence or confidence motion.
Floor test where majority is disputed.
Defeat on an expressly treated confidence issue.

groups.heading: LOSS AND TRANSITION
items: Resign or seek lawful dissolution.
Constitutional head may assess a viable alternative.
Caretaker government preserves continuity with restraint.

stages.answer_line: In the Article 356 context, legislative majority should ordinarily be tested on the Assembly floor rather than inferred from subjective claims outside the House; proclamation material is judicially reviewable.

stages.title: CABINET, COUNCIL AND PRIME MINISTERIAL LEADERSHIP

groups.heading: COUNCIL
items: The wider constitutional ministry includes several ranks.
All share collective responsibility.
The Council is not identical to the Cabinet.

groups.heading: CABINET
items: Smaller inner decision core.
Handles policy, legislation, budget and crisis choices.
Cabinet Committees specialise coordination.

groups.heading: PRIME MINISTER
items: Selects and allocates portfolios through advice.
Chairs Cabinet and leads the majority or coalition.
Connects President, ministry and Parliament under Article 78.

stages.mechanism_strip: The Cabinet Secretariat page accessed on 24 August 2026 confirms business-rule administration, Cabinet assistance and inter-ministerial coordination.
stages.answer_line: Article 123 permits temporary legislation when Parliament is not in session, but repeated or strategic ordinances can bypass deliberation and weaken legislative accountability.

stages.title: PARLIAMENTARY ACCOUNTABILITY AND EXECUTIVE DOMINANCE

groups.heading: LEGISLATIVE SCRUTINY
items: Questions, debates, motions and confidence devices.
Budget, grants and financial committees.
Bill and delegated-legislation committees.

groups.heading: WIDER CORRECTIVES
items: CAG-PAC chain and constitutional offices.
Opposition, media, Rajya Sabha and elections.
Judicial review and transparency law.

groups.heading: RISKS / REFORM
items: Whip and anti-defection pressure limit dissent.
Compressed sittings and information asymmetry weaken scrutiny.
More time, information and committee capacity improve responsibility.

stages.answer_line: Declining deliberation calls for stronger sittings, committees and scrutiny practices, not abandonment of a parliamentary system whose accountability mechanisms remain constitutionally available.

stages.title: PARLIAMENTARY VERSUS PRESIDENTIAL GOVERNMENT

groups.heading: PARLIAMENTARY
items: Fusion and interdependence.
Ministry survives on House confidence.
Continuous accountability and flexible replacement.

groups.heading: PRESIDENTIAL
items: Organisational separation.
President normally has a fixed term.
Tenure stability, but possible deadlock.

groups.heading: INDIAN PRECISION
items: India combines parliamentary responsibility with federalism and review.
UK has orthodox parliamentary sovereignty.
US has a separately elected executive.

stages.answer_line: Secretaries are accountable within the executive and subject to oversight, law and confirmation structures, but the President's tenure does not depend on lower-House confidence.

stages.title: INDIAN ADAPTATION, COALITIONS AND CURRENT DEBATE

groups.heading: WHY ADOPTED
items: Familiarity and continuity.
Accommodation of diversity through legislature.
Daily responsibility and flexible government change.

groups.heading: INDIAN EXPERIENCE
items: Coalition bargaining can broaden inclusion.
Minority governments intensify confidence politics.
PM dominance and anti-defection can weaken deliberation.

groups.heading: CURRENT CONTROL
items: The 129th Amendment Bill remains under committee review.
Proposed Article 82A is not current text.
Use simultaneous elections only for system analysis.

stages.answer_line: India chose a responsible executive dependent on legislative confidence because continuous accountability and coordination were preferred to an independently fixed presidential tenure.
